We have thought of that, and my hon. friend will find that the wording of the item is entirely satisfactory. These reductions will apply to British goods as well, if they should he found in any case to affect them. But these oases will be found to be very few. They will ajpply, however, not only to the United States but they will apply to every country with which we have what is called the favoured nation treaty. It is well understood that by virtue of these old treaties (many of them made years ago at a time when Canada had hardly reached its present mature status, and when the colonies were not so consulted as they are now in regard to these arrangements), these old treaties still outstanding and binding the whole empire oblige us to give whatever is given to one country to all other countries possessing these treaties. We have had that question repeatedly up here, and hon. gentlemen no doubt understand it. And so, these reductions wall have to be given in each ease to the various countries which have what is called the favoured nation treaties.
It is too soon to make any very close examination into the financial results, but

I thought we ought to make an approximate estimate and that it would interest the House to know what that estimate is. As far as we can see on a hurried examination, on the basis of last year's business-assuming that for the first year under the operation of this arrangement the volume of trade to be the same as last year,- it would result in a reduction of taxation amounting to $2,260,000. Therefore, even from the point of view of the reduction of the burden on the taxpayer the matter is well worthy of attention.
We have been impressed, Mr. Speaker, from the beginning-my hon. colleague the Minister of Customs and myself, who have been charged with these negotiations-with the great importance of the matter. I need hardly say we have given to the work our best consideration and attention. We have fortunately had the benefit of the assistance of two capable and able officers of our public service. I refer to Mr. John McDougald, the Commissioner of Customs, or Deputy Minister of Customs as he really is, and Mr. James A. Russell, for many years in the Customs department, but now assigned to the tariff branch of the Finance Department. In the preparation of the information necessary for an intelligent study of this question, and later on in the working out of the details of the arrangement, we have received from these gentlemen a service of the utmost value, and I desire in this public way, to express how deeply we are indebted to them.
It would be too much to expect that an arrangement of this character should be adopted without careful criticism and perhaps it is too much to expect that it should be passed without adverse opinion. The common experience is that all grave and important movements are calculated sometimes to alarm people and that we are amazed afterwards as the years roll on to find how our anticipations have not been realized. I trust it will be found by those who have been somewhat anxious, perhaps nervous, possibly alarmed for the outcome of. these negotiations; I trust as they look into the matter carefully, they will find, as I believe they will find, that their anxiety, while very natural, was hardly necessary. In this arrangement, they will find that every interest in the Dominion of Canada has received our careful consideration. We hope indeed to broaden the trade between our neighbours and ourselves; we have desired to find larger markets for our products. We are doing that all the time; we are sending our commercial agents to the uttermost ends of the earth to seek for business; why not seek it from the 92,000,000 people who live side by side with [DOT] us ?
We present this arrangement as one Mr. FIELDING.
which we feel we can sincerely commend to the judgment of this House and of the people of Canada. We do not present it to the House as something in which we have won a victory over our American friends. That, Sir, would be a small return for the good spirit in which they have met us. I desire to say that throughout these negotiations the President of the United States has given us abundant reason to appreciate his sincere desire to carry out a friendly arrangement. He will carry into the completion of this transaction the authority of his great office and his great talents; he will carry into it, Sir, all the energy and ability he possesses to bring it to a successful issue, and I know he will make it a labour of love.
And, no less commendable has been the line of conduct of the distinguished Secretary of State of the United States, Mr. P. C Knox. As this is an international matter, it came under the direction of the Secretary of State. Mr. Knox gave it close personal attention for many days, day after day, and I know he is not less anxious than the President of the United States to bring about a friendly arrangement. From these two distinguished gentlemen, from every oflicer of the State department and Treasury department, and from all with whom we were brought in contact we found abundant evidence of an honest and sincere desire to make a friendly arrangement with us.
We present the arrangement to you to day, Sir, not as a triumph of one country over the other, but as the result of an effort to do justice to both; we commend this arrangement, Sir, to the judgment of this parliament as the President of the United States will commend it to the judgment of the Congress. The one fear I have is that there may be people who will say that we have made so good a bargain that the Congress should not approve of it. In times past friendly arrangements have been made with the United States government which have failed to receive the approval of the Congress, 'but we think the time is more favourable now. We think we have found the psychological moment for dealing with this question; we think we are within reach of some of the commercial advantages for which our people have struggled now for half a century. We commit this matter to the care of the Canadian parliament with the firm conviction that it is going to be a good thing for Canada, a good thing for the United States, and that we will continue to have it and maintain it not because there is any binding obligation to do so, but because the intelligence of the people of the two countries will decide that it is a good thing for the promotion of friendly relations and for the development of commerce of the two countries.

Resolution to be moved in Committee of Ways
and Means.
That it is expedient to amend the Customs Tariff, 1907, and to provide as follows:-
1.	That the articles, the growth, product or manufacture of the United States, specified in schedule A shall be admitted into Canada free of duty when imported from the United States.
2.	That the articles, the growth, product or manufacture of the United States, specified in schedules B and 1 * shall be admitted into Canada upon payment of the rates of duty specified in the said schedules when imported from the United States.
That the advantages hereby granted to the United States shall extend to any and every other foreign power which may be entitled thereto under the provisions of any treaty or convention with His Majesty.
That the advantages hereby granted to the United States shall extend to the United Kingdom and the several British colonies and possessions with respect to their commerce with Canada. Provided however, that nothing herein contained shall be held to increase any rate of duty now provided for in the British preferential tariff.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not, of course, at the present moment attempt to follow the Minister of Finance in a detailed examination of the proposals which he has presented to parliament. The first thing that strikes one in connection with these proposals is that they are of a very far-reaching and comprehensive character and that they amount in many respects to a proposal to parliament to enact an entirely new tariff. What their effect may be upon many industries in Canada and especially on many of the smaller industries scattered all over the country I would not attempt to-day to suggest. Looking at them as the Minister of Finance presented them to the House, I was inclined to think that the conditions of trade as they kre in Canada at the present time will be subject to very serious interference and dislocation from these proposals. Probably there is no man in this House of Commons to-day, not even the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Customs, who can foresee with any reasonable degree of accuracy just what the effect upon our trade conditions may be in the future as resulting from these changes.
One or two observations, however, of a general character I would like to make. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has referred to the. history of reciprocal relations with the United States of America. He has said very truly that we in this country must always have regard to the fiscal policy of a great nation numbering nearly one hundred millions of people, whose boundaries adjoin ours for nearly 4,000 miles. I entirely agree with that. And I would like to suggest to my hon. friend that we ought, also, to have earnest and serious regard to our relations with the three hundred millions of people who are under the British flag with ourselves. But when the Minister of Finance spoke of the history of reciprocal relations with the United States in the past he might well have drawn a moral and a lesson which he did not draw in the spirit in which he addressed this House to-day. Let us look for a moment at that treaty of reciprocity which existed between the British North American colonies and the United States between 1854 and 1866. What were the conditions of trade during that period, and what followed the denunciation of that treaty by the United States? Certain lines of trade and of industry were established in this country during the years in which that treaty was in force. When that treaty was denounced my right hon. friend remembers, and most of the members of this House remember, that intense confusion was wrought in all conditions of life in Canada by the fact that that treaty was denounced upon one year's notice. Canada
did not realize at that time her strength. Canada, it is true, did not then possess the strength which she possesses to-day. But Canada encountered that situation with a firm and confident spirit, and after many years of progress and development under a policy laid down by the Liberal-Conservative party in 1878, and carried out almost unimpaired by the gentlemen who now sit upon the treasury benches, Canada occupies a position at the present time which does not seem to call for the active interference with our fiscal conditions which has been proposed to this House.
Mr. Speaker, what has been the song, what has been the cry, of the Minister of Finance, of the Minister of Customs, and of the Prime Minister himself, in this parliament? During the past eight or ten years they have been telling us over and over again, in every budget speech to which I have listened, that the conditions of Canada were so absolutely satisfactory that every good and true Canadian ought thoroughly to rejoice therein. Canada found new markets after the denunciation of the reciprocity treaty, she found those markets for the most part within the limits of the British Empire, she found markets which she might confidently believe would be open to us, not only now, but in all the years to come. Well, Sir, what does the Minister of Finance propose to-day? He proposes an arrangement of a very far-reaching and comprehensive character, which will bring about a considerable dislocation in the business interests of this country; there is no doubt at all about that. What does he say as to the duration of that arrangement? He says it is expected that this arrangement will continue for a considerable time. Nothing could be more indefinite. My hon. friend the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) asked the Minister of Finance a question, which was upon my own lips; he asked: Is this an indivisible agreement? Does it mean everything that is contained in these resolutions and these schedules, everything or nothing? The Minister of Finance answered that by saying, in a rather indefinite and hesitating way, that he supposed, so far as he understood the situation, that it meant everything or nothing. Well. I would think that the Minister of Finance should be able to give to parliament, in presenting a statement of this important and far-reaching character, the certain meaning of this treaty in that regard. My hon. friend from South York asked the minister another important question, which had also occurred to me. Suppose the Dominion of Canada, next year, or the year after, or five years from now, interfered with one single item set forth in these schedules, or with half a dozen items contained in them, what would

be the net result upon the understanding which has been arrived at between the two countries? In that respect, also, the answer of the Minister of Finance left it open to every member of this House to draw whatever conclusion he might see fit. The answer was no answer at all, and we. do not know at this moment, the Minister of Finance has not seen fit, or is not able to say, what the result would be upon this understanding between the two countries if, in two years from now, the parliament of Canada saw fit to alter or amend the customs duties in respect to half a dozen of these items.

speechtext: This parliament will be absolutely free to do what it likes, the United States congress and this parliament are both absolutely free. This is an arrangement to which we are committed 'because we believe it is for the good of both countries ; and if one year hence we make up our minds, one country, or the other, that this arrangement is not mutually beneficial, we will change it, that is all.

speechtext:
Well I am bound to say that that seems to be an extraordinary arrangement, an arrangement of a most indefinite and unsatisfactory character, an arrangement the duration of which is uncertain, the character of which is uncertain, and the effects of which are uncertain-except that we are assured that they will in the immediate future dislocate the conditions which the government have pronounced for many years past to ibe absolutely satisfactory to the people of this country.
Now, let us look for a moment at the reasons which have impelled the government to enter into this arrangement. My hon. friend was exceedingly frank; he told the House, and very truly, that the government of this country, almost against their will, had 'been forced into making this arrangement by the suggestions from the United States that they intended to impose their maximum tariff, whereupon the government of Canada, only a year ago, saw fit to recede from the attitude they had held down to the opening of last session. My hon. friend" placed himself and his government in an exceedingly curious position toy one remark he made to-day. He said that it would have been the duty of the President of the United States to withhold the minimum tariff from Canada unless the concessions which were made toy this parliament last year had been agreed to by Canada, and in the next breath he said that these concessions were of so paltry and trivial a character that the people of Canada need not toe concerned with them at all. Now, will any hon.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax!.
gentleman in this House tell me that the President of the United States would have felt himself constrained to hold the tariff of Canada, -without those paltry and trivial concessions, as unjust or discriminatory towards the United States? Why, the mere statement of the case is sufficient to refute the argument of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in that regard, and to show the people of Canada that if the government had stood firm at their post as they promised to do at the commencement of last year they would not have been obliged to make the concessions of last session or to engage in the reciprocity negotiations, the result of which has 'been brought down by the hon. Minister of Finance to-day. That is the true history of these negotiations, as I understand it.	.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has said that the proposals winch he submits to parliament may be roughly divided under three considerations; in the first place, that the arrangements are to be carried out by mutual legislation, and not by treaty, in the second place that there is a large free list which consists chiefly of natural products and, in tne third place, that a uniform rate of duty is to be imposed by the two countries upon many articles which are enumerated in one of the schedules. Well, Sir, he has mentioned some articles that are free and he has mentioned some upon which there is to be a uniform duty. In so far as some of the items are concerned, for example, that of agricultural implements, I do not believe that the reduction of the duty upon agricultural implements, which he proposes, will yield the slightest iota of relief to any of the farming population of tnis country, and I am convinced that the price which will be charged the farmers in the future will not be affected in the slightest degree whatever by the reductions which he proposes to make in that regard. The Minister of Finance has referred to several important articles of agricultural production which are to be admitted duty free into the United States. We will discuss those later on. He has referred to the importation into the United States of fish free of duty and he has said that the government of Canada has declined to extend to the fishermen of the United States access to our fishing grounds. That also will be discussed later on. He says that the government of this country denied the United States free fishing. I would like to tell the Minister of Finance and the government that the fishermen of the Unued States at the present time enjoy free fishing in many Canadian waters simply for the reason that those waters are not protected as they ought to be.

I think, Mr. Speaker, that the policy of Canada in fiscal matters ought to be regulated and directed solely with a view to the interests of the Canadian people as a whole. I understand and I thoroughly appreciate the importance of good relations with the United States of America. The United States of America have fixed tneir tariff in the past and they will fix it at all times in the future purely from the standpoint of the interests of their own people and the development of their own country. It is our duty in Canada to do precisely the same thing. We have had in this country, since 1878 or 1879, a policy which lias sought to protect and develop our own natural resources by the labour of our own people. The object of any government in this country ought to be to accomplish that good and desirable- result without imposing any oppressive burdens on the people as a whole, and the Conservative party has stood, and it stands today, for a policy of that kind. The Conservative party stands to-day, as it stood in the past, for the policy of reciprocity within this great British Empire. As far as we are concerned we believe that the aim and object of the fiscal legislation of this country ought to be to promote that great end and object, and we believe that, for that purpose, as well as for the purpose of fiscal freedom in every possible respect, we ought to keep ourselves free of all entangling treaties, or alliances, or understandings; that that object and purpose, which I regard as the greatest consideration that could be before the -eyes of any Canadian statesman to-day, should be kept constantly before our minds and that _ everything that would lessen the possibility, probability or imminence of carrying out that great scheme of reciprocity within the empire ought to be banished from our minds and put aside as unworthy of our attention.
Then, there is another consideration, Mr. Speaker, which, I think, ought to be borne in mind. As a natural result of the policy to which I have alluded-the policy of building up our own country, developing our own resources and keeping our people at home-we have had the lines of communication in the past running from east to west and not from north to south. They have run from the Atlantic to the Pacific, they have not stopped at the Atlantic or the Pacific, but they have stretched across both oceans, and I see in the proposals which the government has brought down to-day a purpose and object which seems to me to be absolutely inconsistent with that which has been, as I have understood, the purpose and object of the Canadian people for the last thirty years at least. I do not regard it as a good omen
for the future of Canada that the government of the day should seek to alter that condition and to divert those lines of trade and communication, now running from east and west so that they shall run in the future from north to south. We have spent a great deal of money in this country, we have taxed our resources perhaps as the resources of no other people in the world were ever taxed to carry out the policy, the object and purpose to which I have alluded, and if there is any meaning at all in the proposals of the government to-day they mean the almost absolute and complete reversal of that purpose and object.
One would have thought that the present was an especially inopportune time for taking up tariff negotiations with the United States; in the first place, because the tariff of the United States, as is well known, is very much higher than our own in very many important articles indeed; and, for the further very good jmd important reason that if you can judge at all from the trend of public opinion in the United States, the probability is that the tariff of the United States will be revised and very largely reduced upon many of those articles which are enumerated in the schedules brought down by the Minister of Finance.
The negotiations, in short, are a sequel to the surrender which this government made last year. I am, at the same time, of the opinion that if our government had then stood firm the government of the United States would never have imposed their maximum tariff against Canada.
In conclusion, while not able to apprehend the full meaning and scope of these proposals or the exact results which will ensue from this tariff policy now proposed, I believe it is open to severe and grave criticism by reason not only of the considerations which I have very briefly addressed to the House this afternoon, but by reason of the fact that it does not, sufficiently regard the position of this country as an integral and important nation of the British Empire and does not sufficiently regard the purpose, the object and scope of the policy to which Liberals and Conservatives alike, as I understand the records of the past have been committed with respect to the development of Canada and its status as a nation of the British Empire.
At six o'clock, House took recess.

House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.

speechtext:
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to authorize the Governor in Council to, on or after the seventh of April, 1911, grant a subsidy for steamship service between a port or ports on the Pacific coast of Canada and China and Japan, for such period or periods of time as may be deemed expedient, not however to exceed in the aggregate ten years, and to pay therefor a subsidy or subsidies, as the case may be, not exceeding the sum of 25,000 pounds sterling per annum for such service as may be deemed expedient from time to time.
He said: The House will understand this resolution when I say it is to renew the subsidy which has been voted for some years past to the Canadian Pacific railway for the service which is now well' known between Vancouver and Japan and China,
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the resolution.

subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.
speechtext: How long has this arrangement been in force?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
The subsidy
was put in force shortly after the Canadian Pacific railway was completed and has been continued for some 20 years. It has been renewed once. The subsidy has been contributed by the Canadian and the imperial governments. We are not certain yet whether or not the imperial government will continue their contribution, but we are in communication with them on the subject.

subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.
speechtext: What boats are engaged in this service?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.
speechtext: There are three boats, the ' Empress of China,' the ' Empress of Japan,' and the ' Empress of India.' The service is about every twentieth day and the speed of the boats fifteen knots.

subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.
speechtext: I saw some reference in the press to the refusal of this government to co-operate with the governments of Australia or New Zealand with respect to some such service.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
No, it is quite the reverse. My hon. friend refers to the Australian service. There is another line of steamers subsidized from Vancouver to Australia and New Zealand. That service has been in operation now for several years. We are renewing it now. There has been some difference between the governments of Australia and New Zealand. New Zealand is contributing a very large sum but the government of Australia has refused up to the present Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
to again aid this service unless there is direct communication with them, avoiding the port in New Zealand. We thought it would not be advisable to give up the service to New Zealand. We have offered the governments of Australia and New Zealand to renew the service just as it was, simply with an improved service, but up to the present time the government of Australia has not thought fit to join. We are in hopes, however, they may be persuaded to do so. At all events, we have endeavoured to maintain the service even if it be confined to Canada and New Zealand.

subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.
speechtext:
That is a distinct service from this?
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Absolutely.

subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.
speechtext: We should have some information about this service, whatever the expectations in connection with it have been realized, whether the trade with China and Japan has greatly improved, for instance, in wheat and fruit stuffs. We should also know what provision there is for the carriage of perishable products, whether there is cold storage and whether we have any control over the freight rates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.
speechtext: There is no arrangement for cold storage on the boats. The result as to improvement of trade has not been very much. We have some trade with Japan which has been increasing to some extent. Our trade with China has made very little progress, if any. Notwithstanding this, I believe that at the present time it would be very unfortunate if these services were abandoned, when China is developing very rapidly, and when Japan is also developing. The little trade we have with those countries would then go to San Francisco, and I think it is worth the sacrifice we are making to keep that trade in our own hands.

subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.
speechtext: A few years ago there were trial shipments of flour to China and Japan, and rather bright anticipations were held out about the trade that we ought to develop along that line. It was said that it would be a veTy valuable trade to the Northwest. We ought to have some information as to whether that trade is being established or not, or whether -we are making the proper efforts to get it.

subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CHINA-JAPAN STEAMSHIP SUBSIDY.
speechtext: The suggestion that we should have cold storage on the ships is a very reasonable one. The conditions of the contract between the government and the company have not yet been adopted. We are merely asking here for the authority of parliament to renew the contract. I will report to my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce the suggestion that has been made. I can give to my hon. friend the information that he asked as to the character of the steamers.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: It has been stated in the press that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company intend to place larger boats on the Pacific next summer, I presume for this service. This proposal is to renew the contract for at least ten years, which would mean subsidies aggregating $1,250,000. This is a contract which has been in operation for several years, and the wisdom of parliament must be exercised to determine whether it be wise to renew it or not or whether, if it be renewed, different terms should not be insisted on. That can only be judged by the results we have had in the past, and for that purpose I desire to find out whether the trade has been developing from year to year and to what extent and in what lines. Many years ago when we agreed to give subsidies to certain steamship lines, we provided that they should be equipped with cold storage and we had an agreement with them as well regarding the rates. But, if I correctly understand the present position, the government do not seem to be taking any precaution in that line whatever, and thus we may be giving a big subsidy which may practically bring us no profit. If there be little or no trade, our subsidy will be so Tnuch money thrown away. To enable us to judge whether it be wise to vote this large amount for the next ten years we should know more about what have been the results under the contract about to terminate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: I shall give all that information at the next stage.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext:
I would like to be allowed to insist upon the cold storage provision.
Undoubtedly, whatever may have been the results in the past, there is a very large cold storage trade to be done with the east. Large quantities of our perishable products are required in China, and these can only be sent there in steamers provided with cold storage. I think it would be proper, in a contract of this magnitude, to stipulate that cold storage facilities must be provided and further that the rates should be under the control of the government or the Railway Commission. Otherwise this company may charge the same rates to shippers as if they were receiving no subsidy whatever from the government. If they want to do that trade, they will have to equip their vessels with cold storage in any case; and when we give them a subsidy, they should be obliged, not only to provide that cold storage, but to submit their rates to the control of this government. Some time ago I heard a complaint regarding lumber shipments on these steamers. In the eastern ports lighters are used to take the lumber from the steamers to the shore, and it appears that the lighter charges were such as to render the sihipment unprofitable, It would, therefore, be necessary to stipulate in the contract that the lighter charges should be moderate and not such as to make the trade unprofitable.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext:
I agree that when the steamers, the 'Empress of Japan' and the 'Empress of China,' were put on the line between Vancouver and the eastern ports, the refrigerator system was not what it is to-day. But the Canadian Pacific Railway authorities are contemplating putting new steamers on that service. My

hon. friend from Jacquees Cartier (Mr. Monk) will see, by the last annua] report of the Canadian Pacific railway, that its president, Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, announced that before long new steamers would 'be put on that route. In 1891, and the years immediately following, when we gave a subsidy to the Canadian Pacific railway, the company was practically depending on its return cargoes of silk and tea, because practically there was no trade from this country to the east on the outward voyage except the tourist business. Since then, however, the Canadian Pacific railway has recognized that it must put larger steamers on this route equipped with the most modern refrigerator system. So far the company has given good service, but my hon. friend is quite justified in saying that the refrigerator service requires to be improved on account of the increasing trade in perishable products between the far east and Canada.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: I have noticed that the Canadian Pacific railway contemplate improving that service, but we are now about to make a contract with it, and that contract will be made long before these new steamers are in operation. At any rate the point regarding cold storage should have the attention of the government. If we are going to give this large subsidy, we should reserve control over the freight rates on perishable products, as otherwise our trade will languish, whereas the American trade with the east is in full bloom and vigour. I do not know whether my hon. friend the Postmaster General, during his travels in the east, noticed whether the lumber was taken ashore in lighters.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: They invariably use lighters to tranship their freight to the wharfs. As regards perishable products, I notice that the apple trade is growing immensely with Japan and China, and also the cheese trade. I told the exmember for Perth (Mr. McLaren), that I had seen some of his cheese in Tokio and Yokohoma, but it had been shipped on American boats, just because there were no refrigerators on board our steamers. The point taken, therefore, by my hon. friend was well taken.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: The complaint I particularly made was with regard to the special rates charged by the lighters, and these rates, in spite of the protests of the shippers, are persisted in by the Canadian Pacific railway. It would ibe necessary to guard against that by providing that the freight rates would cover the carriage from port to port irrespective of these additional charges. Such subsidies should be made absolutely conditional upon our control of the freight rates.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: Do we pay an additional subsidy to these boats for carrying the mails ?

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: The mail contracts are made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and revised by the Post Office Department, but the subsidy is for the mails.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: Is the subsidy simply for the carriage of the mails and not for the purpose of stimulating trade?

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: The subsidy is supposed to be not only for the carriage of the mails but to stimulate the development of trade between the two countries, just as in the case of the Atlantic service.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: These subsidies are not paid only for carrying the mails?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: The main object of the subsidy is to encourage trade.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: If the subsidy was merely for the carriage of the mail there would be no need to stipulate about cold storage.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: And no need of such a large subsidy either.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: This legislation will give the Governor in Council authority to spend $125,000 a year for ten years and the government should be able to tell us what the extent and nature of the trade it is expected will be developed with China and Japan. Usually, when we ask what trade has been developed by the voting of these large subsidies for steamers to different parts of the world the government have to answer that the development of trade was not as large as they expected. Again, I would suggest that although the resolution gives the government power to contract for ten years it would be much better to make the contract for five years so that parliament might have An opportunity to say at the end of the shorter period whether it was wise to continue the subsidy or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: This is of course merely for the renewal of the subsidy. My own personal view is that in the immediate future I do not expect there will be much development of trade as a result of this subsidy, but I certainly do expect that some years hence we shall have a large and gfowing trade with the Orient.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: In what class of goods?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext:
I should think in cereals, lumber, fruit, manufactured products, minerals such as lead, and as the Orient, Japan especially, is coming more and more to western civilization, I should think we would have a large trade

in machinery with Japan and possibly with China. I shall remember the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) that possibly it would not be wise to make a contract for ten years. Certainly I would be inclined somewhat to his view that the term should be five years.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: Can the Prime Minister say how this would affect Prince Rupert as a Pacific port?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: Sufficient for the day is the evil or the good thereof. It is quite possible that when Prince Rupert has come to be the terminus of the new Transcontinental line we may have to adopt the same policy with regard to it that we do with regard to the Canadian Pacific railway.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: How many trips a year are we now getting for the subsidy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: About eighteen.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: This is a very considerable subsidy and I am inclined to believe that even if there was no subsidy it would be impossible for a wealthy and powerful corporation like the Canadian Pacific railway to abandon that part of its round-the-world route, and that it would be necessary for them to maintain that steamship line for the next ten years. However I believe with my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) that ten years is a very long period to contract for. It would be more satisfactory if the contract were laid upon the table of the House for approval before it was finally entered into; so that we may see whether these features in connection with the freight rates and cold storage are carefully safeguarded. What information I have received would lead me to believe that there would be a very much larger movement of lumber from the province of British Columbia towards the east if it had not been that the rates charged were absolutely unreasonable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: The points raised by my hon. friends somewhat commend themselves to my judgment and I think I will be able to answer them at the next stage of the Bill.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext:
When the next stage comes we shall have information as to what progress has been made in the quantity of freight taken in and out during the last twenty years and as to what class of goods have been carried. I sympathize with the Prime Minister and the rest of the government in the matter of the small amount of information we have been aDle to draw from them. It is almost wonderful how little ministers may know when they come to ask parliament for a subsidy of $125,000 a year for ten years, to a company like this. We can see from the blue-book reports what the trade with China and Japan
is, but it would be very instructive to know what proportion of that trade comes by these subsidized steamers. If it should turn out to be that but a small proportion is being carried by them it might need investigation as to the cause, and if it shall be found to be due to high freight rates that should be guarded against. The Postmaster General told us that no allowances were paid to these steamers for the mails, and that it was included as one of the duties they were to perform in earning the subsidy. Is it the same in the case of the carriage of the British mails. What arrangement is there now about the mails between Great Britain and China and Japan? Who pays the cost of carriage across from port to port?

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: I could not exactly say, but there is a large amount paid by the imperial authorities, and then there is a subsidy by the Trade and Commerce Department, which includes the Canadian mails taken by the Canadian Pacific railway.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: Suppose the minister traces it from London, how does it come?

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: It comes by our Atlantic steamers, by the Canadian Pacific railway or the Allan steamers, to whom we pay subsidies.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: Are we paying for the British mails?

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: No, not for British mail coming here, but we pay for Canadian mails going out. The British government is paying for British mails coming in. The mails are taken off the steamer by the Intercolonial railway as far as Montreal or Quebec.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: For which the Intercolonial railway gets paid?

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: The Intercolonial railway gets a proportion.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: Where does the Intercolonial railway gets its proportion from?

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: That depends. If all the mails are delivered at the Rimouski wharf, then they are taken to Quebec, where they are delivered to the Canadian Pacific railway, or to Montreal, and then the Intercolonial railway get a proportion for carrying them from Rimouski to that point. Then the mails are taken by the Canadian Pacific railway straight on to Vancouver, where they are delivered on the Canadian Pacific railway boats and carried across.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: Then for a British mail starting from Liverpool or other British port, the British government pays the cost of passage across the Atlantic?

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: It then goes on the Intercolonial railway, and is handed to the Canadian Pacific railway at Quebec. Does the British government pay for the cost of their jpail, the China and Japan mail, on the Intercolonial railway?

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: I could not give the figures to my hon. friend, but there is an arrangement made by the two governments at the end of every fiscal year, and adjustment as regards the proportion.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: The object of the adjustment is that the British government shall pay for its through mails whatever that carriage costs. What I want to get at is whether we are mixed up with their accounts."

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: No, we have a special contract.

subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext: It seems to me the time has come for us to consider whether we ought not to adopt the same system as they have in England, and I think in the United States, where they pay so much for carrying the mails, irrespective of any trade considerations. Trade subsidies are not given to ships in England nor in the United States. With us the situation is different. I am not opposed in principle to subsidizing steamship lines for trade purposes, but I think that those purposes to be entirely distinct from- the carriage of mails. We ought to adopt the system they have in those countries, where they have more experience than we have, and pay for the carriage of mails distinct from all other purposes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DESCRIPTION OF VESSELS EMPLOYED ON THE CANADA, CHINA AND JAPAN SERVICE.
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend that the time may have arrived when we should revise our mail subsidies between Canada and Great Britain. But my hon. friend knows under what conditions these subsidies were paid, in the infancy of steam navigation, when Sir Hugh Allan organized a service between Canada and Great Britain. The Canadian government at that time decided, and I think very properly, to give special inducements to the enterprise of Sir Hugh Allan. At that time Canada had not a population like that of the United States or of Great Britain. There had been no necessity at all for giving a special subsidy for the encouragement of that line for trade purposes, trade alone was sufficient to induce enterprising merchants to organize such a service. But we did it with a view of getting a mail service between Canada and Great Britain. This steam service has been going on something like sixty years.
Mr. LEMIEUX
My hon. friend says we should revise that system, and I do not dispute it. I think the time has well come when we may, perhaps, think of having a mail service between Canada and Great Britain on the rule of paying so much per ton. Now, with regard to our trade with the Orient. Some time after the completion of the Canadian Pacific railway it was thought advisable to give them a special subsidy to help them to put on a service between Vancouver and China and Japan. This subsidy is not given exclusively for the carriage of mails; it is given in excess of what would be a legitimate compensation for carrying the mails. But it was done to encourage trade, and to establish communication between Canada and the Orient. I am bound to say that that trade has not developed_ to the extent we had expected. But I think no one at this moment would desire to abandon that service. We think it ought to be maintained, even if it has not done all we expected from it; at all events, we think it better to leave it as it is. subtopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUA1 AND OTHER DRUGS.

speechtext:
Hon. AIACKENZIE KING moved second reading of Bill (No. 97) to prohibit the improper use of opium and other drugs. He said: Air. Speaker, the House will remember that a year or two ago a Bill was introduced into and passed by this parliament having for its purpose the suppression of the opium traffic in Canada. That Bill came as a result of the inquiry which took place on the Pacific coast shortly after the riots which had occurred, affecting the conditions of the Chinese and Japanese residing in the city of Vancouver. A number of Chinese whose stocks of opium had been somewhat damaged in those riots put in claims for losses which they had suffered in the
[DOT]2519

manufacture of opium. Those claims came as a surprise to a good many people in this country, who were not aware that the opium traffic was making any headway on this continent, particularly in Canada. Upon the report of the inquiry which I had the privilege of making, a Bill was introduced by the then Minister of Labour, the Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux, for the purpose of prohibiting the manufacture, sale and importation of opium. So far as the manufacture of opium is concerned that Bill has proved most effective. Where there were seven factories operating in different cities on the Pacific coast three years ago, there are none at the present time ; so that the manufacture of opium in Canada has been completely suppressed by that legislation, and the importation has been very largely suppressed. On the other hand, it has been found that in spite of the regulations, a considerable amount of opium has been smuggled into Canada. The police have found that the present legislation is not drastic enough, or broad enough, to give them the powers of seizure and confiscation which they regard as necessary. One of the objects of the present Bill is to make more drastic the regulations in that regard. Before submitting this Bill to the House I conferred with the chiefs of police in Vancouver and Montreal, two officers who have had a good deal of experience in administering the law, and obtained from them suggestions which are embodied in the Bill.
The legislation of two years ago did not prohibit opium smoking. It was thought, that as parliament was prohibiting the importation of opium. the smoking of opium would itself cease. But this has not proven to be the case, foT it is found that the practice of opium smoking is considerable in a good many of the cities of Canada. The present Bill prohibits absolutely the smoking of opium.
I would like to bring to the attention of the House the international aspect of this question. In 1909 an international commission met in Shanghai for the purpose of considering whether it was possible for the different nations of the world to assist the Chinese government in its efforts to suppress the opium traffic ifl China. As is generally known, it is estimated that something like 20,000,000 people in that empire are victims of the opium habit, and the Chinese government, recognizing the importance of a strong manhood to the nation, has sought to eradicate the evil and has asked other nations to join with it in the effort to suppress the opium traffic. At that international commission some 13 or 14 different countries were represented. It was the first international commission which has ever assembled in the Orient. The British Empire had five representa-Mr. KING.
tives including one from this country. After a careful investigation and series oi reports from the several delegations the International Commission adopted a series of resolutions which the various delegates were asked to present to their respective governments in the hope that these governments would give effect to them. I shall read those resolutions, inasmuch as we are seeking, by the Bill before the House, to give effect to those resolutions so far as Canada is concerned. The first resolution relates to the efforts which the Chinese government is making to suppress the opium traffic, and is in the following words :
That the International Opium Commission recognizes the unswerving sincerity of the government of China in their efforts to eradicate the production and consumption of opium throughout the empire, the increasing body of public opinion among their own subjects by which these efforts are being supported, and the real, though unequal, progress already made in a task which is one of the greatest magnitude.
The second resolution is:-
That in view of the action taken by the government of China in suppressing the practice of opium smoking, and by other governments to the same end, the International Opium Commission recommends that each delegate concerned move its own government to take measures for the gradual suppression of the practice of opium smoking in its own territories and possessions, with due regard to the varying circumstances of each country concerned.
It may be of interest to the people of this country to know that when that International Commission met in Shanghai it was possible for the example of this country to be cited as one to be followed by other nations. It was pointed out that that example had been followed by the United States, and the commission hoped that it would be followed by other countries. The third resolution is:-
That the International Opium Commission finds that the use of opium in any form otherwise than for medical purposes is held by almost every participating country to be a matter for prohibition or for careful regulation; and that each country in the administration of its system of regulation purports to be aiming, as opportunity offers, at progressively increasing stringency. In recording these conclusions, the International Opium Commission recognize the wide variations prevailing in the different countries, but it would urge on the attention of the governments concerned the desirability of a re-examination of tbeir systems of regulation in the light of experience with other countries dealing with the same problem.
That is what we are doing in considering this measure.
The fourth resolution expresses the need for co-operation between the nations, and 'is as follows :
That the International Opium Commission finds that each government represented has

strict laws which are aimed directly or indirectly to prevent the smuggling of opium, its alkaloids, derivatives and preparations into their respective territories; in the judgment of the International Opium Commission it is also the duty of all countries to adopt reasonable measures to prevent at ports of departure the shipment of opium, its alkaloids, derivatives and preparations, to any country which prohibits the entry of opium, its alkaloids, derivatives and preparations.
The fifth resolution relates to the other drugs than the particular one referred to as opium and its alkaloids. It was recognized in this gathering, composed of men who had given careful study to the question, that as the opium traffic was suppressed other drugs equally dangerous might take its place, such as morphine and cocaine, and the commission took fihe ground that it was desirable that every country which sought to suppress the opium habit should also pass effective legislation with respect to other habit-forming drugs. It is found that the morphine and cocaine habits prevail in some of our cities to an extent which, to say the least, is distressing. I mention these two drugs because of the bearing of the fifth resolution of the commission on the proposed legislation, which resolution I will now read :
In the present Bill will be found a clause with this object in view :
That the International Opium Commission finds that the unrestricted manufacture, sale and distribution of morphine already constitutes a grave danger, and that the morphine habit shows signs of spreading. The International Opium Commission therefore desires to urge strongly on all governments that it is highly important that drastic measures should be taken by each government in its own territories and possessions to control the manufacture, sale and distribution of this drug, and also of such other derivatives of opium as may appear on scientific inquiry to be liable to similar abuse and productive of like ill effects.
In this report of the International Opium Commission, which held meetings at Shanghai from February 1, to February 26, 1909, we have the recommendation on the part of the representatives of thirteen different countries that each should pass legislation which would effectively suppress, not merely the habit of opium eating and smoking, but also the habits that are formed in connection with such drugs as morphine and cocaine. The parliament of Canada, by passing the legislation now proposed will, therefore, be assisting not merely to put down the evil in this Dominion, but will be taking part in a world wide movement which has for its object the suppression of this kind of evil in all countries.

Of course in a matter of this kind the experience of physicians and of those who have to do with the sale of drugs is all important, and I would, therefore, ask permission to quote part of the speech delivered by the president of that association on that occasion. It will be found on page 4 of the report under the subject heading ' Control of the Supplies of Narcotic Poisons.' :
The control of supplies of narcotic poisons, notably cocaine might profitably engage your attention, and your deliberations should quite properly lead to a request to the federal government to consider the advisability of enacting measures to more completely safeguard the public from the harmful consequences of unregulated use of these dangerous drugs. It is futile to attempt to restrict the supply of these drugs in the absence of general and effective measures throughout the domain. The welfare of our public demands that inviolable laws be enacted by the parliament of our country to make it impossible to procure these peculiarly degrading drugs for any but legitimate professional treatment. As to the proper medium of supply, it is clearly evident that the trained and legally qualified pharmacist is the one person indicated for this function and control by conditions established by govermental regulation through co-operation with your association. This logically suggests the need of a Dominion Pharmacy Act, and as this aspect of the question is to come before you in another relationship, nothing further in this regard is necessary for my present purpose. The necessity for closer restrictions on narcotic drugs of less marked character than those usually recognized as dangerous might he dealt with at this section. It must have come within observation of more than one pharmacist that much harm and misery is wrought by uncontrolled use of even so apparently innocent a preparation as paregoric. There is no logical reason why it should not he sold subject to the same condition as other preparations of opium.
In addition to those two reports from specially qualified sources, I might give to the House information which has come to me unsolicited within the last few weeks from different parts of this country. The number is indeed amazing of the communications which have come to the department from all quarters since it became generally known that legislation of this kind was proposed. These communications all go to show the serious character of the evil we are endeavouring to deal with and the urgent need of immediate legislation. I have a letter sent me to-day by the Dominion parole officer, Mr. Archibald, who has had a good deal of experience with criminals as they

leave the prisons, and he says in this letter -which incloses a confidential communication under consideration by another department:
It is only one of many I come in contact with, and I am safe in saying that 12 to 15 per cent of all the young prisoners I come in contact with credit these drugs with the cause of their downfall.
There you have the statement by General Staff Inspector Archibald that from 12 per cent to 15 per cent of the young prisoners he comes in contact with attribute their downfall to drugs. He adds:
I am grateful for humanity's sake that something is contemplated for relief of a system which is taking hold of many of our best young men and bringing in its train the consequent ruin to both the mental and physical life in our Dominion. Had I time and opportunity to make a census of prisons, I would be greatly surprised if the percentage would not reach over 25 per cent of their populations rather than the figures quoted from my actual experience.
When I communicated with the Chief of Police in Vancouver and sent him a copy of the Bill which I proposed with regard to opium, this is what he replied:
November 21, 1910.
Dear Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your telegram of the 19th inst., having reference to the Dominion Act

I had previously discussed this subject with Chief Chamberlain, in Vancouver, and communicated with him by wire when about to 'bring this measure before my colleagues.
I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your telegram of the 19th inst., having reference to the Opium Act, and asking for suggestions from me with a view of amending the same, and in reply beg to state that I would strongly recommend the following amendments :-
1st. It should be an offence for any one to he found smoking opium. At the present time it is not an offence.
2nd It should be an offence for any person to he found in possession of opium other than a qualified druggist or doctor.

Then in reply to a communication I addressed to Mr. O. - Campeau, the chief of police in Montreal, I received the following: Montreal, December 10, 1910.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your communication of recent date asking if 1 had any suggestions to offer in connection with the Bill which was introduced in the House of Commons to prohibit the importation, manufacture, sale and use of opium, and especially as regards the best means of suppressing the opium traffic and the evils growing out of same.
I took communication of the Bill, and in my opinion its dispositions shall contribute iu a great measure to the suppression of that disastrous traffic.
I wish, 'however, to call your attention to another traffic which, since about six months, spread devastation in this city especially. I mean to say the trade of cocaine.
Since six months the Montreal police have made over one hundred and twenty-five arrests of persons for selling or using that drug.
As you know, the only legislation which-applies to the sale of cocaine is the Pharmaceutical Act of this province, and the penalties enacted for its violation are very lenient.
The fact that the violation of this law is growing up so rapidly and with so disastrous effects shows evidently that the present legislation is not effective.
Therefore, without offering specific suggestions concerning the Bill presently before the House of Commons for consideration, I will ask if it would not be possible to include in this Bill the cocaine and other drugs.
According to the medical men the cocaine produces worse effects than opium, and it would be a good occasion to adopt proper legislation to suppress the cocaine traffic and the evils growing out of same.
One of the means whereby information is gathered by the Department of Labour in relation to matters affecting industrial and social conditions is the selection from newspapers of items which are classified and kept for reference. I have here a very large number of such clippings referring to this subject, but I shall only read one or two to indicate the nature of the reports which have recently appeared in the press. In the Montreal ' Witness ", of November 23, 1910, under the heading ' Cocaine a Social Plague ' there is an account of some convictions that took place before Mr. Recorder Dupuis who is reported to have used the following language:
'This curse of cocaine,' proceeded Mr. Recorder Dupuis, speaking with emphasis, 'has existed for a short time in the city. It is a

real evil. It is a social plague, and it goes on spreading so fearfully tiiat it is time for society to take marked notice. Alcoholism and morphia are nothing to cocaine. It is the agent for the seduction of our daughters and the demoralization of our young men. 1 should be a doctor if I could tell you all the evil that exists in it. Those who know what cocaine is and what its evils are,- are those who can hurt society most. If the chemists themselves do not give us a hand to assist in stopping the habit we can do nothing. There is no remedy. The able lawyer who represents the Pharmaceutical Association has asked for tine to be increased from $25 to $100. This would not help us at all. As it is now, cocaine is sold at $12 the ounce, and the profits made thereby are stupendous. A num-oer of doctors, who know all the evils of cocaine, must be prescribing it right and left. I wish legislation would be passed so that chemists would have to be licensed in the same way that alcohol dealers are, and licenses could then be refused to those who went on selling cocaine. It is a crime against society. I know of my own knowledge a doctor who says that of ten chemists he knows, six sell cocaine, one he is not sure of, and the remaining three do not. Those who sell it are nothing short of conspirators against society. The College of Physicans and Surgeons should take the matter up. It would be a good thing if chemists were not allowed to sell cocaine without taking the names and addresses of buyers, so that it would be easy, if desired, to find out what doctor had given the prescription. As to selling without prescriptions, that should be positively forbidden.
'For the love of a few dollars these men have thrown away the lives and futures of young men and young girls. I said formerly that those who put foreign matter or water into milk were criminals. Well, I find no word adequate for those who poison the very life blood of society. I am giving the alarm. I call upon parliament, upon the legislature and upon our representatives to do all in their power to stamp it out.'
The 'Montreal Star' of November 17, 1910, has an article headed ' Much cocaine is sold here in an illegal way,' and it gives an account of the existence of the traffic in Montreal. I also think it should he made a criminal offence the same as opium is. It will only he necessary to inform you that at the last meeting of our association held at Halifax in September, a strong resolution was adopted urging tbe federal parliament to recognize the imperative demand for legislation prohibiting or controlling the sale of all 'habit-forming' drugs and narcotics throughout the Dominion.

I learned through the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) that Mrs. Henderson, of Montreal, the probation officer of the Children's Aid Society had given this subject very careful study during the past year or two, and I wrote Mrs. Henderson asking if she could come to Ottawa and give the government the benefit of her investigations into the existence of the evil. The story told by Mrs. Henderson was a very sad one indeed. She reported that of her own observation she had met as many as fifty or sixty little girls and boys within the same day, in the city of Montreal, all of whom had acquired the cocaine habit to some degree. She spoke of little girls taken out of cocaine dens, and of young hoys whose whole futures had been blighted. It is a fact that this cocaine has been distributed amongst school children and that to-day in that city many a parent is having an anxious time for -his child because of the contraction of this habit. I believe that to no person in Canada is so much credit due for the agitation against cocaine as to Mrs. Henderson, of Montreal, who has devoted her time willingly and persistently in an attempt to suppress this great evil. While I do not want to take up time, I feel it my duty to insist as emphatically as I can against the adoption of this section. By this Bill we are creating new criminal offences, and this section proposes to vest in the Governor in Council the power, by simply adding the name of any substance whatever to this schedule, to make the possession, the handling in any way of such substance a criminal offence. I most earnestly urge upon the minister the impropriety of parliament delegating this most serious power to the Governor in Council.
It is an exceedingly grave thing for parliament to take the practical omnipotence it holds as a legislative body and hand it over to be exercised absolutely by the Governor in Council; it is asking the council not an executive, but a legislative body. The answer that similar provision is incorporated in other legislation is not to me a conclusive reason. Some one has said by way of criticism of the English system of law resting upon precedent that under it, when a man once went wrong he forfeited forever after the right to be right. However that may be with English jurisprudence, there is certainly no such limitation on this parliament to follow precedent, and I would strongly suggest to the minister that he should strike out this section. We have one exceedingly bad precedent in the other Bill already cited, and I do not think we should let it go down from precedent to precedent. Iam of course strongly in favour of the legislation before us, but when we hand'oyer to the government the power to make innocent acts, crimes, it really means the abdication by parliament of the power the constitution confided to it and to it alone. Certainly, between the sessions of parliament there is hardly a sufficient time for a new evil to assume such vicious proportions as to call for legislation to suppress it, and that being so what possible public danger is there in leaving it to parliament each session to deal with the evils that may have grown up in the interval ? If we might expect new evils of this nature to spring up from day to day, there might be something to be said in favour of conferring

this power on the Governor in Council but one may very well hope that human ingenuity is not going to be so determinedly devoted to finding new methods of debauching the people of this country as to make it impossible for us to keep apace with it in legislation from session to. session. I speak with a good deal of earnestness in this matter, because I cannot conceive anything more undesirable in the way of legislation, and because each repeated instance will afford an additional argument for doing it again until we will have added to what are the legitimate functions of the Governor in Council, practically the enactment of the criminal law.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUA1 AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext:
In view of the opinion expressed by so eminent a jurist as my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty), it is with diffidence that I still urge the retention of this section. I should hesitate to do so on my own responsibility, but the point has been carefully considered by the law advisers, who have thought it desirable to give this power to the Governor in Council. After all whatever is done by the Governor in Council, so far as criminal legislation is concerned, would be done upon the advice of the Minister of Justice, who, it may be expected, will zealously safeguard the administration of the criminal law were there any probability of this power being abused. I would withdraw the section were there likely to be any doubt as to the intention of parliament in the matter, but in naming the three drugs, cocaine, morphine and opium, parliament makes it plain that it is legislating against what are known as habit-forming drugs, and it recognizes that as from time to time, one form of the drug is suppressed, a derivative of it may rapidly spring up which it is desirable to check as speedily as possible. We have similar provisions in the Patent Medicine Act and in the Act dealing with noxious weeds. The business of parliament is becoming more considerable every year. Larger and more important subjects are constantly coming to the fore and require all the time and attention that can be given them. We should seek to limit rather than add to the number of measures to be brought up for consideration. Suppose it were found that between sessions one noxious weed had cropped up somewhere that was not named in the schedule attached to the Act respecting noxious weeds. Also one new proprietary medicine not named in the schedule to that Act, and one drug not named in this, all of which should be legislated against. New Acts would have to be introduced in each case and with the growing business of parliament it would be found impossible in time to go into such detailed legislation. For these reasons, I think it is desirable to allow the section to remain.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-SUPPLY OF STERILIZED WATER IN PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform you and the members of the House what has been done to secure a supply of safe drinking water for the use of
the members and officials of the House. The department has had installed in the building a process for sterlizing the water. This is done by a machine which is manufactured by the Forbes Sterilizer. Company. Since the machine has been installed and this process adopted we have had samples of the water tested. On the 11th of this month we sent 11 samples, which were taken from the sterilizing apparatus and from each of the faucets on the different floors, both on the House of Commons and the Senate side. The report is that these samples failed to show any growth and that the water supplied by the Forbes Sterilizers may now be considered perfectly safe. It is not desirable to take water from the tap in this chamber though I think it has not been com-ipletely turned off. We have on each floor a tap which carries the water direcuy from the cooler. The water is sterilized and then cooled so that it is quite agreeable for drinking. I think it is not desirable that any ice should be used in the water, but I trust that arrangements may be made by which the vessels containing the water may be surrounded with ice so that it may be kept even cooler than at present. The report we have is that the water is perfectly safe. Of course it is very necessary that care should be exercised by the officials of the House, and this morning a letter was sent to the clerk of the House as follows:
Dear sir,-In view of the present eqidemic of typhoid in the city of Ottawa it is necessary that the utmost care be taken in connection with the drinking water. I enclose a copy of a memorandum prepared for me by the Superintendent of Dominion Buildings stating the steps recently taken by this department to prevent such a contingency in the parliament buildings, and I would suggest that arrangements be made so that only sterilized water be used in the receptacles in the buildings.
(Signed) J. B. HUNTER,
Deputy Minister.
I have not seen the Sergeant at Arms, but I spoke to the deputy sergeant and he informs me that the pages have been instructed to take water only from the taps that lead from the sterilizer, so it is quite safe to send for water.
